- The Black-Scholes (or Black-Scholes-Merton) model is a mathematical model of the dynamics of a financial market containing derivative instruments, from whose parabolic partial differential equation one deduces the Black-Scholes formula: a theoretical price for European-style options that is unique given the security's risk, with the security's expected return replaced by the risk-neutral rate.
- Black-Scholes prices an option by hedging it: buying and selling the underlying asset continuously so as to eliminate risk, a technique called continuously revised delta hedging, which is the basis of the more complicated hedging strategies used by investment banks and hedge funds.
- Volatility is the only Black-Scholes parameter that cannot be observed directly in the market; because the option value rises with it for both puts and calls, the formula can be inverted on observed option prices to produce a volatility surface, which is then used to calibrate other models.
- Louis Bachelier's 1900 thesis was the earliest publication to apply Brownian motion to derivative pricing, but it had little impact for many years and carried important limitations for application to modern markets.
- Black and Scholes invented the risk-neutral argument in 1968 by showing that dynamically revising a portfolio removes the security's expected return; they then lost money trying to trade the formula for lack of risk management, returned to academia in 1970, and published it in 1973 as "The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities" in the Journal of Political Economy.
- Merton and Scholes received the 1997 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for the risk-neutral dynamic revision, which the committee credited with separating the option from the risk of the underlying security; Black, who died in 1995, was ineligible but named as a contributor.
- Black-Scholes assumes the riskless asset earns a constant rate of return, the risk-free interest rate.
- Black-Scholes assumes the stock price follows a geometric Brownian motion with constant drift and volatility; if drift and volatility vary with time a modified formula can still be derived, provided the volatility is not random.
- The Black-Scholes market assumptions are: no arbitrage opportunity, unlimited borrowing and lending of fractional amounts of cash at the riskless rate, unlimited buying and selling of fractional amounts of the stock including short selling, and no fees or costs on any of those transactions.
- Several original Black-Scholes assumptions have been removed by later extensions: modern versions account for dynamic interest rates (Merton, 1976), transaction costs and taxes (Ingersoll, 1976), and dividend payout.
- The Black-Scholes equation is the parabolic partial differential equation governing the option price V(S,t), where S is the underlying price, t is time, sigma is volatility and r the risk-free rate: dV/dt + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + rS dV/dS - rV = 0.
- The financial insight behind the Black-Scholes equation is that the option can be perfectly hedged by trading the underlying asset and cash so as to eliminate risk, which is what implies a unique option price.
- The Black-Scholes call price for a non-dividend-paying stock is C(S_t,t) = N(d+)S_t - N(d-)K e^{-r(T-t)}, with d+ = [ln(S_t/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)(T-t)] / (sigma sqrt(T-t)) and d- = d+ - sigma sqrt(T-t).
- The Black-Scholes put price follows from put-call parity rather than a separate derivation: P(S_t,t) = K e^{-r(T-t)} - S_t + C(S_t,t) = N(-d-)K e^{-r(T-t)} - N(-d+)S_t.
- The Black-Scholes formula is obtained by solving the Black-Scholes equation subject to the terminal and boundary conditions C(0,t)=0 for all t, C(S,t) ~ S - K e^{-r(T-t)} as S goes to infinity, and C(S,T)=max{S-K,0}, which is why the formula and the equation are consistent with each other.
- In the Black-Scholes formula N(x) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, N(x) = (1/sqrt(2 pi)) times the integral of e^{-z^2/2} from minus infinity to x.
- Time to maturity in the Black-Scholes notation is tau = T - t, the difference between the option's expiration time T and the current time t.
- Introducing the discount factor D = e^{-r tau} and the forward price F = e^{r tau} S = S/D simplifies the Black-Scholes call to C(F,tau) = D[N(d+)F - N(d-)K], a special case of the Black '76 formula, in which d+ = [ln(F/K) + (1/2)sigma^2 tau] / (sigma sqrt(tau)).
- Put-call parity in forward terms is C - P = D(F - K) = S - DK, and it yields the put price P(F,tau) = D[N(-d-)K - N(-d+)F].
- The Black-Scholes call decomposes into two binary options -- long an asset-or-nothing call, short a cash-or-nothing call -- which is what the two terms of the formula are: a call exchanges cash for an asset at expiry, an asset-or-nothing call yields the asset with no cash exchanged, and a cash-or-nothing call yields cash with no asset delivered.
- Reading N(d+) and N(d-) as probabilities of the option expiring in the money is incorrect, because either both binaries expire in the money or neither does, so a single event cannot carry two different probabilities.
- The cash-or-nothing term of the Black-Scholes formula does read as probability times value, because the cash payoff is independent of the underlying's movements; the asset-or-nothing term does not, because the probability of expiring in the money and the asset's value at expiry are not independent unless the numeraire is changed from cash to the asset.
- The (1/2)sigma^2 term that distinguishes d- from standardized moneyness m = ln(F/K)/(sigma sqrt(tau)) comes from the gap between the median and the mean of the log-normal distribution -- the same factor Ito's lemma produces for geometric Brownian motion.
- N(d-) is the probability that a Black-Scholes call is exercised when the asset is assumed to drift at the risk-free rate, whereas N(d+) has no simple probability interpretation; N(d+) is correctly read as the present value, at the risk-free rate, of the expected asset price at expiration conditional on that price exceeding the strike.
- The probabilities appearing in the Black-Scholes formula are measure-theoretic probabilities under the equivalent martingale (risk-neutral) measure, and neither is the true probability of expiring in the money under the real physical measure; computing that requires additional information, the drift.
- The Feynman-Kac formula says the appropriately discounted solution of the Black-Scholes PDE is a martingale, so the option price is the expected value of its discounted payoff -- the risk-neutrality approach, which prices options without any knowledge of PDEs.
- The Greeks measure the sensitivity of a derivative's or portfolio's value to a change in one parameter with the others held fixed; they are the partial derivatives of the price with respect to those parameters, and one Greek may be the partial derivative of another, as gamma is of delta.
- Financial institutions typically set risk limits on each of the Greeks that their traders must not exceed, which is why the Greeks matter to trading and not only to the mathematical theory of finance.
- Gamma and vega take the same value for a call and a put on the same underlying, because the difference between a put and a call is a forward, which is linear in S and independent of sigma and therefore has zero gamma and zero vega.
- Greeks are usually quoted scaled to the size of a likely parameter change: rho divided by 10,000 for a one-basis-point rate move, vega divided by 100 for a one-volatility-point move, and theta divided by 365 or 252 for one day of decay on calendar or trading days.
- For an instrument paying a continuous dividend yield q, the Black-Scholes call is C(S_t,t) = e^{-r(T-t)}[F N(d1) - K N(d2)] with forward F = S_t e^{(r-q)(T-t)}, an assumption that is reasonable for options on indices.
- Under discrete proportional dividends, where a fraction delta of the stock price is paid out at predetermined times, the stock is modelled as S_t = S_0 (1-delta)^{n(t)} e^{ut + sigma W_t} with n(t) the number of dividends paid by time t, and the call price keeps its usual form with forward F = S_0 (1-delta)^{n(T)} e^{rT}.
- Pricing an American option is the optimal stopping problem of choosing when to exercise, so the Black-Scholes equation becomes a variational inequality: the PDE expression is at most zero, the option value is at least the payoff H(S), and V(S,T) = H(S) at expiry.
- The American variational inequality generally has no closed-form solution, though an American call on a non-dividend-paying stock equals the European call, and the Roll-Geske-Whaley method solves the case of an American call with one dividend.
- For a perpetual American put the time decay is zero, so the Black-Scholes PDE collapses to the ordinary differential equation (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + (r-q)S dV/dS - rV = 0, which does admit a closed-form solution even though the finite-maturity American put does not.
- The perpetual American put is worth V(S) = K/(1-lambda2) [(lambda2-1)/lambda2]^{lambda2} (S/K)^{lambda2} above the exercise boundary S- = lambda2 K/(lambda2 - 1), below which exercising is optimal.
- A cash-or-nothing call, which pays one unit of cash if the spot is above the strike at maturity, is worth C = e^{-r(T-t)} N(d2); the corresponding asset-or-nothing call, paying one unit of asset, is worth C = S e^{-q(T-t)} N(d1).
- A binary cash-or-nothing call is the limit of an infinitesimally tight call spread, so its value is the negative derivative of the vanilla call price with respect to strike: C = -dCv/dK.
- Taking the volatility skew into account, a binary call is worth C = C_no-skew - Vega_v * Skew, where the skew is the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike; a typically negative skew therefore raises the binary call's value.
- Skew matters far more for binary options than for vanilla options, because the Black-Scholes model relies on a symmetric distribution and ignores the skewness of the asset's distribution.
- Because a binary call is the derivative of a vanilla call with respect to strike, the price of a binary call has the same shape as the delta of a vanilla call, and the delta of a binary call has the same shape as the gamma of a vanilla call.
- For foreign exchange, paying one unit of domestic currency when the spot is above or below the strike is exactly a cash-or-nothing call or put, and paying one unit of foreign currency is exactly an asset-or-nothing call or put, giving digital values C = e^{-r_d T} N(d2) for the domestic payout and C = S e^{-r_f T} N(d1) for the foreign payout.
- The Black-Scholes assumptions are not all empirically valid, and blindly following the model exposes the user to unexpected risk; its most significant limitations are underestimating extreme moves (tail risk), assuming instant cost-less trading (liquidity risk), assuming a stationary process (volatility risk), assuming continuous time and trading (gap risk), and underpricing deep out-of-the-money while overpricing deep in-the-money options.
- Delta hedging alone suffices to hedge an option inside the Black-Scholes model, but in practice there are many other sources of risk.
- Black-Scholes pricing remains widely used because it is a useful approximation for the direction prices move when crossing critical points, a robust basis for more refined models, and reversible -- price can be treated as an input and volatility solved for, giving the implied volatility used as a quoting convention.
- If the Black-Scholes model held, a stock's implied volatility would be identical across all strikes and maturities; in practice the volatility surface is not flat, which is how the model can be tested and found wanting.
- The shape of the implied volatility curve depends on the underlying: equities are skewed, with implied volatility substantially higher for low strikes and slightly lower for high strikes than at-the-money; currencies are more symmetrical, lowest at-the-money and higher in both wings; commodities often behave the reverse of equities.
- The standard practice despite the volatility smile is to treat the volatility surface as a fact about the market and feed an implied volatility from it into a Black-Scholes valuation, an approach described as using "the wrong number in the wrong formula to get the right price".
- Black-Scholes cannot be applied directly to bonds because of pull-to-par: as the bond approaches maturity all its prices become known and its volatility falls, which the model does not reflect.
- Interest rate volatility can contribute significantly to an option's price, especially a long-dated one, because rates vary by tenor and over time while Black-Scholes takes a single constant rate.
- Black-Scholes assumes positive underlying prices and does not work directly when the underlying can go negative; practitioners then use a different model such as Bachelier's, or add a constant offset to the prices.
- Haug and Taleb argue that Black-Scholes merely recasts existing widely used models in terms of practically impossible dynamic hedging rather than risk, to make them compatible with mainstream neoclassical economic theory, and assert that Boness published an actually identical formula in 1964.
- Warren Buffett wrote in his 2008 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders that the Black-Scholes formula, though the standard for establishing the dollar liability for options, produces strange and even absurd results when applied to long-dated valuations.
- Ian Stewart said Black-Scholes had underpinned massive economic growth and that by 2007 the international financial system was trading derivatives valued at one quadrillion dollars per year, calling the equation the mathematical justification for that trading.
- The normality assumption of the Black-Scholes model does not capture extreme movements such as stock market crashes.
- The Black-Scholes delta, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying price, is N(d+) for a call and N(d+)-1 for a put -- equivalently -N(-d+) -- so a call's delta lies between 0 and 1 and a put's between -1 and 0.
- The Black-Scholes gamma, the second partial derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying price, is N'(d+)/(S sigma sqrt(T-t)), where N' is the standard normal density.
- The Black-Scholes vega, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to volatility, is S N'(d+) sqrt(T-t).
- The Black-Scholes theta, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to time, is -S N'(d+) sigma / (2 sqrt(T-t)) - r K e^{-r(T-t)} N(d-) for a call and -S N'(d+) sigma / (2 sqrt(T-t)) + r K e^{-r(T-t)} N(-d-) for a put: the two differ only in the sign of the second term.
- The Black-Scholes rho, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to the risk-free rate, is K(T-t) e^{-r(T-t)} N(d-) for a call and -K(T-t) e^{-r(T-t)} N(-d-) for a put.
- The Black-Scholes Greeks are available in closed form and are obtained by differentiating the Black-Scholes formula, which is why every sensitivity of the model is exactly computable rather than estimated numerically.
- The original Black-Scholes model assumes the stock pays no dividend, though trivial extensions of the model can accommodate a continuous dividend yield factor.
- Delta is the most important Greek because it usually carries the largest risk, and many traders zero their delta at the end of the day when they are not speculating on market direction, following the delta-neutral hedging approach Black-Scholes defines.
- "Vega" is not a letter of the Greek alphabet; the name arose from misreading the Greek letter nu.
- Black and Scholes showed for the European call and put that it is possible to create a hedged position -- long the stock, short the option -- whose value does not depend on the price of the stock, which is the result the whole model rests on.
- Substituting N(d-) for N(d+) in the Black-Scholes formula yields a negative value for out-of-the-money call options, which is a direct demonstration that the naive reading of the two terms as one probability times one value is wrong.
- d+ and d- are measures of moneyness expressed in standard deviations, and N(d+) and N(d-) are the probabilities of expiring in the money in their respective numeraires -- the stock for the first, the risk-free asset for the second.
- Barone-Adesi and Whaley approximate the American option by splitting the stochastic differential equation into the European option value plus the early exercise premium, then solving a quadratic for the premium under some assumptions; the solution requires finding the critical underlying price at which one is indifferent between exercising early and holding to maturity.

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0001
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes (or Black-Scholes-Merton) model is a mathematical model of the dynamics of a financial market containing derivative instruments, from whose parabolic partial differential equation one deduces the Black-Scholes formula: a theoretical price for European-style options that is unique given the security's risk, with the security's expected return replaced by the risk-neutral rate.
Topics: option pricing, derivatives

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0002
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black-Scholes prices an option by hedging it: buying and selling the underlying asset continuously so as to eliminate risk, a technique called continuously revised delta hedging, which is the basis of the more complicated hedging strategies used by investment banks and hedge funds.
Topics: hedging, delta hedging

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0003
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Volatility is the only Black-Scholes parameter that cannot be observed directly in the market; because the option value rises with it for both puts and calls, the formula can be inverted on observed option prices to produce a volatility surface, which is then used to calibrate other models.
Topics: implied volatility, calibration

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0004
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Louis Bachelier's 1900 thesis was the earliest publication to apply Brownian motion to derivative pricing, but it had little impact for many years and carried important limitations for application to modern markets.
Topics: history of finance

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0005
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black and Scholes invented the risk-neutral argument in 1968 by showing that dynamically revising a portfolio removes the security's expected return; they then lost money trying to trade the formula for lack of risk management, returned to academia in 1970, and published it in 1973 as "The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities" in the Journal of Political Economy.
Topics: history of finance

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0006
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Merton and Scholes received the 1997 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for the risk-neutral dynamic revision, which the committee credited with separating the option from the risk of the underlying security; Black, who died in 1995, was ineligible but named as a contributor.
Topics: history of finance

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0007
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black-Scholes assumes the riskless asset earns a constant rate of return, the risk-free interest rate.
Topics: model assumptions

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0008
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black-Scholes assumes the stock price follows a geometric Brownian motion with constant drift and volatility; if drift and volatility vary with time a modified formula can still be derived, provided the volatility is not random.
Topics: model assumptions, geometric Brownian motion

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0009
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes market assumptions are: no arbitrage opportunity, unlimited borrowing and lending of fractional amounts of cash at the riskless rate, unlimited buying and selling of fractional amounts of the stock including short selling, and no fees or costs on any of those transactions.
Topics: model assumptions, frictionless market

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0010
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Several original Black-Scholes assumptions have been removed by later extensions: modern versions account for dynamic interest rates (Merton, 1976), transaction costs and taxes (Ingersoll, 1976), and dividend payout.
Topics: model extensions

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0011
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes equation is the parabolic partial differential equation governing the option price V(S,t), where S is the underlying price, t is time, sigma is volatility and r the risk-free rate: dV/dt + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + rS dV/dS - rV = 0.
Topics: Black-Scholes equation, PDE

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0012
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The financial insight behind the Black-Scholes equation is that the option can be perfectly hedged by trading the underlying asset and cash so as to eliminate risk, which is what implies a unique option price.
Topics: replication, no arbitrage

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0013
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes call price for a non-dividend-paying stock is C(S_t,t) = N(d+)S_t - N(d-)K e^{-r(T-t)}, with d+ = [ln(S_t/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)(T-t)] / (sigma sqrt(T-t)) and d- = d+ - sigma sqrt(T-t).
Topics: Black-Scholes formula, call option

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0014
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes put price follows from put-call parity rather than a separate derivation: P(S_t,t) = K e^{-r(T-t)} - S_t + C(S_t,t) = N(-d-)K e^{-r(T-t)} - N(-d+)S_t.
Topics: put-call parity, put option

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0015
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes formula is obtained by solving the Black-Scholes equation subject to the terminal and boundary conditions C(0,t)=0 for all t, C(S,t) ~ S - K e^{-r(T-t)} as S goes to infinity, and C(S,T)=max{S-K,0}, which is why the formula and the equation are consistent with each other.
Topics: boundary conditions, PDE

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0016
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: In the Black-Scholes formula N(x) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, N(x) = (1/sqrt(2 pi)) times the integral of e^{-z^2/2} from minus infinity to x.
Topics: notation

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0017
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Time to maturity in the Black-Scholes notation is tau = T - t, the difference between the option's expiration time T and the current time t.
Topics: notation

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0018
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Introducing the discount factor D = e^{-r tau} and the forward price F = e^{r tau} S = S/D simplifies the Black-Scholes call to C(F,tau) = D[N(d+)F - N(d-)K], a special case of the Black '76 formula, in which d+ = [ln(F/K) + (1/2)sigma^2 tau] / (sigma sqrt(tau)).
Topics: Black 76, forward price

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0019
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Put-call parity in forward terms is C - P = D(F - K) = S - DK, and it yields the put price P(F,tau) = D[N(-d-)K - N(-d+)F].
Topics: put-call parity

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0020
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes call decomposes into two binary options -- long an asset-or-nothing call, short a cash-or-nothing call -- which is what the two terms of the formula are: a call exchanges cash for an asset at expiry, an asset-or-nothing call yields the asset with no cash exchanged, and a cash-or-nothing call yields cash with no asset delivered.
Topics: binary options, interpretation

Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Reading N(d+) and N(d-) as probabilities of the option expiring in the money is incorrect, because either both binaries expire in the money or neither does, so a single event cannot carry two different probabilities.
Topics: interpretation

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0022
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The cash-or-nothing term of the Black-Scholes formula does read as probability times value, because the cash payoff is independent of the underlying's movements; the asset-or-nothing term does not, because the probability of expiring in the money and the asset's value at expiry are not independent unless the numeraire is changed from cash to the asset.
Topics: numeraire, interpretation

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0023
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The (1/2)sigma^2 term that distinguishes d- from standardized moneyness m = ln(F/K)/(sigma sqrt(tau)) comes from the gap between the median and the mean of the log-normal distribution -- the same factor Ito's lemma produces for geometric Brownian motion.
Topics: moneyness, Ito's lemma

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0024
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: N(d-) is the probability that a Black-Scholes call is exercised when the asset is assumed to drift at the risk-free rate, whereas N(d+) has no simple probability interpretation; N(d+) is correctly read as the present value, at the risk-free rate, of the expected asset price at expiration conditional on that price exceeding the strike.
Topics: risk-neutral measure, interpretation

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0025
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The probabilities appearing in the Black-Scholes formula are measure-theoretic probabilities under the equivalent martingale (risk-neutral) measure, and neither is the true probability of expiring in the money under the real physical measure; computing that requires additional information, the drift.
Topics: risk-neutral measure

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0026
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Feynman-Kac formula says the appropriately discounted solution of the Black-Scholes PDE is a martingale, so the option price is the expected value of its discounted payoff -- the risk-neutrality approach, which prices options without any knowledge of PDEs.
Topics: Feynman-Kac, martingale pricing

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0027
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Greeks measure the sensitivity of a derivative's or portfolio's value to a change in one parameter with the others held fixed; they are the partial derivatives of the price with respect to those parameters, and one Greek may be the partial derivative of another, as gamma is of delta.
Topics: Greeks

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0028
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Financial institutions typically set risk limits on each of the Greeks that their traders must not exceed, which is why the Greeks matter to trading and not only to the mathematical theory of finance.
Topics: Greeks, risk limits

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0029
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Gamma and vega take the same value for a call and a put on the same underlying, because the difference between a put and a call is a forward, which is linear in S and independent of sigma and therefore has zero gamma and zero vega.
Topics: Greeks, put-call parity

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0030
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Greeks are usually quoted scaled to the size of a likely parameter change: rho divided by 10,000 for a one-basis-point rate move, vega divided by 100 for a one-volatility-point move, and theta divided by 365 or 252 for one day of decay on calendar or trading days.
Topics: Greeks, market convention

Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: For an instrument paying a continuous dividend yield q, the Black-Scholes call is C(S_t,t) = e^{-r(T-t)}[F N(d1) - K N(d2)] with forward F = S_t e^{(r-q)(T-t)}, an assumption that is reasonable for options on indices.

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0032
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Under discrete proportional dividends, where a fraction delta of the stock price is paid out at predetermined times, the stock is modelled as S_t = S_0 (1-delta)^{n(t)} e^{ut + sigma W_t} with n(t) the number of dividends paid by time t, and the call price keeps its usual form with forward F = S_0 (1-delta)^{n(T)} e^{rT}.
Topics: dividends, single stock options

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0033
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Pricing an American option is the optimal stopping problem of choosing when to exercise, so the Black-Scholes equation becomes a variational inequality: the PDE expression is at most zero, the option value is at least the payoff H(S), and V(S,T) = H(S) at expiry.
Topics: American options, optimal stopping

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0034
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The American variational inequality generally has no closed-form solution, though an American call on a non-dividend-paying stock equals the European call, and the Roll-Geske-Whaley method solves the case of an American call with one dividend.
Topics: American options

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0035
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: For a perpetual American put the time decay is zero, so the Black-Scholes PDE collapses to the ordinary differential equation (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + (r-q)S dV/dS - rV = 0, which does admit a closed-form solution even though the finite-maturity American put does not.
Topics: perpetual options, American options

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0036
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The perpetual American put is worth V(S) = K/(1-lambda2) [(lambda2-1)/lambda2]^{lambda2} (S/K)^{lambda2} above the exercise boundary S- = lambda2 K/(lambda2 - 1), below which exercising is optimal.
Topics: perpetual options, exercise boundary

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0037
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: A cash-or-nothing call, which pays one unit of cash if the spot is above the strike at maturity, is worth C = e^{-r(T-t)} N(d2); the corresponding asset-or-nothing call, paying one unit of asset, is worth C = S e^{-q(T-t)} N(d1).
Topics: binary options

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0038
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: A binary cash-or-nothing call is the limit of an infinitesimally tight call spread, so its value is the negative derivative of the vanilla call price with respect to strike: C = -dCv/dK.
Topics: binary options, call spread

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0039
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Taking the volatility skew into account, a binary call is worth C = C_no-skew - Vega_v * Skew, where the skew is the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike; a typically negative skew therefore raises the binary call's value.
Topics: volatility skew, binary options

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0040
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Skew matters far more for binary options than for vanilla options, because the Black-Scholes model relies on a symmetric distribution and ignores the skewness of the asset's distribution.
Topics: volatility skew

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0041
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Because a binary call is the derivative of a vanilla call with respect to strike, the price of a binary call has the same shape as the delta of a vanilla call, and the delta of a binary call has the same shape as the gamma of a vanilla call.
Topics: binary options, Greeks

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0042
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: For foreign exchange, paying one unit of domestic currency when the spot is above or below the strike is exactly a cash-or-nothing call or put, and paying one unit of foreign currency is exactly an asset-or-nothing call or put, giving digital values C = e^{-r_d T} N(d2) for the domestic payout and C = S e^{-r_f T} N(d1) for the foreign payout.
Topics: FX options, binary options

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0043
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes assumptions are not all empirically valid, and blindly following the model exposes the user to unexpected risk; its most significant limitations are underestimating extreme moves (tail risk), assuming instant cost-less trading (liquidity risk), assuming a stationary process (volatility risk), assuming continuous time and trading (gap risk), and underpricing deep out-of-the-money while overpricing deep in-the-money options.
Topics: model limitations

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0044
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Delta hedging alone suffices to hedge an option inside the Black-Scholes model, but in practice there are many other sources of risk.
Topics: hedging, model limitations

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0045
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black-Scholes pricing remains widely used because it is a useful approximation for the direction prices move when crossing critical points, a robust basis for more refined models, and reversible -- price can be treated as an input and volatility solved for, giving the implied volatility used as a quoting convention.
Topics: implied volatility, market convention

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0046
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: If the Black-Scholes model held, a stock's implied volatility would be identical across all strikes and maturities; in practice the volatility surface is not flat, which is how the model can be tested and found wanting.
Topics: volatility smile, implied volatility

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0047
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The shape of the implied volatility curve depends on the underlying: equities are skewed, with implied volatility substantially higher for low strikes and slightly lower for high strikes than at-the-money; currencies are more symmetrical, lowest at-the-money and higher in both wings; commodities often behave the reverse of equities.
Topics: volatility smile

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0048
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The standard practice despite the volatility smile is to treat the volatility surface as a fact about the market and feed an implied volatility from it into a Black-Scholes valuation, an approach described as using "the wrong number in the wrong formula to get the right price".
Topics: volatility surface, market practice

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0049
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black-Scholes cannot be applied directly to bonds because of pull-to-par: as the bond approaches maturity all its prices become known and its volatility falls, which the model does not reflect.
Topics: bond options, model limitations

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0050
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Interest rate volatility can contribute significantly to an option's price, especially a long-dated one, because rates vary by tenor and over time while Black-Scholes takes a single constant rate.
Topics: model limitations, interest rates

Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black-Scholes assumes positive underlying prices and does not work directly when the underlying can go negative; practitioners then use a different model such as Bachelier's, or add a constant offset to the prices.
Topics: model limitations, Bachelier model

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0052
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Haug and Taleb argue that Black-Scholes merely recasts existing widely used models in terms of practically impossible dynamic hedging rather than risk, to make them compatible with mainstream neoclassical economic theory, and assert that Boness published an actually identical formula in 1964.
Topics: criticism, priority dispute

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0053
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Warren Buffett wrote in his 2008 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders that the Black-Scholes formula, though the standard for establishing the dollar liability for options, produces strange and even absurd results when applied to long-dated valuations.
Topics: criticism

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0054
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Ian Stewart said Black-Scholes had underpinned massive economic growth and that by 2007 the international financial system was trading derivatives valued at one quadrillion dollars per year, calling the equation the mathematical justification for that trading.
Topics: criticism, systemic risk

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0055
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The normality assumption of the Black-Scholes model does not capture extreme movements such as stock market crashes.
Topics: model limitations, tail risk

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0056
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes delta, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying price, is N(d+) for a call and N(d+)-1 for a put -- equivalently -N(-d+) -- so a call's delta lies between 0 and 1 and a put's between -1 and 0.
Topics: Greeks, delta

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0057
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes gamma, the second partial derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying price, is N'(d+)/(S sigma sqrt(T-t)), where N' is the standard normal density.
Topics: Greeks, gamma

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0058
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes vega, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to volatility, is S N'(d+) sqrt(T-t).
Topics: Greeks, vega

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0059
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes theta, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to time, is -S N'(d+) sigma / (2 sqrt(T-t)) - r K e^{-r(T-t)} N(d-) for a call and -S N'(d+) sigma / (2 sqrt(T-t)) + r K e^{-r(T-t)} N(-d-) for a put: the two differ only in the sign of the second term.
Topics: Greeks, theta

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0060
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes rho, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to the risk-free rate, is K(T-t) e^{-r(T-t)} N(d-) for a call and -K(T-t) e^{-r(T-t)} N(-d-) for a put.
Topics: Greeks, rho

Statement: The Black-Scholes Greeks are available in closed form and are obtained by differentiating the Black-Scholes formula, which is why every sensitivity of the model is exactly computable rather than estimated numerically.

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0062
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The original Black-Scholes model assumes the stock pays no dividend, though trivial extensions of the model can accommodate a continuous dividend yield factor.
Topics: model assumptions, dividends

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0063
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Delta is the most important Greek because it usually carries the largest risk, and many traders zero their delta at the end of the day when they are not speculating on market direction, following the delta-neutral hedging approach Black-Scholes defines.
Topics: Greeks, delta hedging, trading practice

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0064
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: "Vega" is not a letter of the Greek alphabet; the name arose from misreading the Greek letter nu.
Topics: Greeks, terminology

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0065
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Black and Scholes showed for the European call and put that it is possible to create a hedged position -- long the stock, short the option -- whose value does not depend on the price of the stock, which is the result the whole model rests on.
Topics: replication, history of finance

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0066
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Substituting N(d-) for N(d+) in the Black-Scholes formula yields a negative value for out-of-the-money call options, which is a direct demonstration that the naive reading of the two terms as one probability times one value is wrong.
Topics: interpretation

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0067
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: d+ and d- are measures of moneyness expressed in standard deviations, and N(d+) and N(d-) are the probabilities of expiring in the money in their respective numeraires -- the stock for the first, the risk-free asset for the second.
Topics: moneyness, numeraire

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0068
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Barone-Adesi and Whaley approximate the American option by splitting the stochastic differential equation into the European option value plus the early exercise premium, then solving a quadratic for the premium under some assumptions; the solution requires finding the critical underlying price at which one is indifferent between exercising early and holding to maturity.
Topics: American options, numerical methods

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0069
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: Bjerksund and Stensland approximate the American option with a trigger-price exercise strategy: exercise is optimal once the underlying reaches the trigger price, and below it the option reduces to a European up-and-out call plus a rebate paid if it is knocked out before maturity; the method is computationally inexpensive and fast.
Topics: American options, numerical methods

unit_id: u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0070
Source: src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3 (family family-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3)
Statement: The Black-Scholes model extends to variable but deterministic rates and volatilities and to European options on dividend-paying instruments, where closed-form solutions survive if the dividend is a known proportion of the stock price; American options and options on stocks paying a known cash dividend are the harder cases.
Topics: model extensions, dividends

Units in this cluster:
- The Black-Scholes (or Black-Scholes-Merton) model is a mathematical model of the dynamics of a financial market containing derivative instruments, from whose parabolic partial differential equation one deduces the Black-Scholes formula: a theoretical price for European-style options that is unique given the security's risk, with the security's expected return replaced by the risk-neutral rate.
- Black-Scholes prices an option by hedging it: buying and selling the underlying asset continuously so as to eliminate risk, a technique called continuously revised delta hedging, which is the basis of the more complicated hedging strategies used by investment banks and hedge funds.
- Volatility is the only Black-Scholes parameter that cannot be observed directly in the market; because the option value rises with it for both puts and calls, the formula can be inverted on observed option prices to produce a volatility surface, which is then used to calibrate other models.
- Black-Scholes assumes the riskless asset earns a constant rate of return, the risk-free interest rate.
- Black-Scholes assumes the stock price follows a geometric Brownian motion with constant drift and volatility; if drift and volatility vary with time a modified formula can still be derived, provided the volatility is not random.
- The Black-Scholes market assumptions are: no arbitrage opportunity, unlimited borrowing and lending of fractional amounts of cash at the riskless rate, unlimited buying and selling of fractional amounts of the stock including short selling, and no fees or costs on any of those transactions.
- Several original Black-Scholes assumptions have been removed by later extensions: modern versions account for dynamic interest rates (Merton, 1976), transaction costs and taxes (Ingersoll, 1976), and dividend payout.
- The Black-Scholes equation is the parabolic partial differential equation governing the option price V(S,t), where S is the underlying price, t is time, sigma is volatility and r the risk-free rate: dV/dt + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + rS dV/dS - rV = 0.
- The financial insight behind the Black-Scholes equation is that the option can be perfectly hedged by trading the underlying asset and cash so as to eliminate risk, which is what implies a unique option price.
- The Black-Scholes call price for a non-dividend-paying stock is C(S_t,t) = N(d+)S_t - N(d-)K e^{-r(T-t)}, with d+ = [ln(S_t/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)(T-t)] / (sigma sqrt(T-t)) and d- = d+ - sigma sqrt(T-t).
- The Black-Scholes put price follows from put-call parity rather than a separate derivation: P(S_t,t) = K e^{-r(T-t)} - S_t + C(S_t,t) = N(-d-)K e^{-r(T-t)} - N(-d+)S_t.
- The Black-Scholes formula is obtained by solving the Black-Scholes equation subject to the terminal and boundary conditions C(0,t)=0 for all t, C(S,t) ~ S - K e^{-r(T-t)} as S goes to infinity, and C(S,T)=max{S-K,0}, which is why the formula and the equation are consistent with each other.
- In the Black-Scholes formula N(x) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, N(x) = (1/sqrt(2 pi)) times the integral of e^{-z^2/2} from minus infinity to x.
- Time to maturity in the Black-Scholes notation is tau = T - t, the difference between the option's expiration time T and the current time t.
- Introducing the discount factor D = e^{-r tau} and the forward price F = e^{r tau} S = S/D simplifies the Black-Scholes call to C(F,tau) = D[N(d+)F - N(d-)K], a special case of the Black '76 formula, in which d+ = [ln(F/K) + (1/2)sigma^2 tau] / (sigma sqrt(tau)).
- Put-call parity in forward terms is C - P = D(F - K) = S - DK, and it yields the put price P(F,tau) = D[N(-d-)K - N(-d+)F].
- The Black-Scholes call decomposes into two binary options -- long an asset-or-nothing call, short a cash-or-nothing call -- which is what the two terms of the formula are: a call exchanges cash for an asset at expiry, an asset-or-nothing call yields the asset with no cash exchanged, and a cash-or-nothing call yields cash with no asset delivered.
- Reading N(d+) and N(d-) as probabilities of the option expiring in the money is incorrect, because either both binaries expire in the money or neither does, so a single event cannot carry two different probabilities.
- The cash-or-nothing term of the Black-Scholes formula does read as probability times value, because the cash payoff is independent of the underlying's movements; the asset-or-nothing term does not, because the probability of expiring in the money and the asset's value at expiry are not independent unless the numeraire is changed from cash to the asset.
- The (1/2)sigma^2 term that distinguishes d- from standardized moneyness m = ln(F/K)/(sigma sqrt(tau)) comes from the gap between the median and the mean of the log-normal distribution -- the same factor Ito's lemma produces for geometric Brownian motion.
- N(d-) is the probability that a Black-Scholes call is exercised when the asset is assumed to drift at the risk-free rate, whereas N(d+) has no simple probability interpretation; N(d+) is correctly read as the present value, at the risk-free rate, of the expected asset price at expiration conditional on that price exceeding the strike.
- The probabilities appearing in the Black-Scholes formula are measure-theoretic probabilities under the equivalent martingale (risk-neutral) measure, and neither is the true probability of expiring in the money under the real physical measure; computing that requires additional information, the drift.
- The Feynman-Kac formula says the appropriately discounted solution of the Black-Scholes PDE is a martingale, so the option price is the expected value of its discounted payoff -- the risk-neutrality approach, which prices options without any knowledge of PDEs.
- The Greeks measure the sensitivity of a derivative's or portfolio's value to a change in one parameter with the others held fixed; they are the partial derivatives of the price with respect to those parameters, and one Greek may be the partial derivative of another, as gamma is of delta.
- Gamma and vega take the same value for a call and a put on the same underlying, because the difference between a put and a call is a forward, which is linear in S and independent of sigma and therefore has zero gamma and zero vega.
- Greeks are usually quoted scaled to the size of a likely parameter change: rho divided by 10,000 for a one-basis-point rate move, vega divided by 100 for a one-volatility-point move, and theta divided by 365 or 252 for one day of decay on calendar or trading days.
- For an instrument paying a continuous dividend yield q, the Black-Scholes call is C(S_t,t) = e^{-r(T-t)}[F N(d1) - K N(d2)] with forward F = S_t e^{(r-q)(T-t)}, an assumption that is reasonable for options on indices.
- Pricing an American option is the optimal stopping problem of choosing when to exercise, so the Black-Scholes equation becomes a variational inequality: the PDE expression is at most zero, the option value is at least the payoff H(S), and V(S,T) = H(S) at expiry.
- The American variational inequality generally has no closed-form solution, though an American call on a non-dividend-paying stock equals the European call, and the Roll-Geske-Whaley method solves the case of an American call with one dividend.
- For a perpetual American put the time decay is zero, so the Black-Scholes PDE collapses to the ordinary differential equation (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + (r-q)S dV/dS - rV = 0, which does admit a closed-form solution even though the finite-maturity American put does not.
- The perpetual American put is worth V(S) = K/(1-lambda2) [(lambda2-1)/lambda2]^{lambda2} (S/K)^{lambda2} above the exercise boundary S- = lambda2 K/(lambda2 - 1), below which exercising is optimal.
- A cash-or-nothing call, which pays one unit of cash if the spot is above the strike at maturity, is worth C = e^{-r(T-t)} N(d2); the corresponding asset-or-nothing call, paying one unit of asset, is worth C = S e^{-q(T-t)} N(d1).
- A binary cash-or-nothing call is the limit of an infinitesimally tight call spread, so its value is the negative derivative of the vanilla call price with respect to strike: C = -dCv/dK.
- Taking the volatility skew into account, a binary call is worth C = C_no-skew - Vega_v * Skew, where the skew is the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike; a typically negative skew therefore raises the binary call's value.
- Skew matters far more for binary options than for vanilla options, because the Black-Scholes model relies on a symmetric distribution and ignores the skewness of the asset's distribution.
- Because a binary call is the derivative of a vanilla call with respect to strike, the price of a binary call has the same shape as the delta of a vanilla call, and the delta of a binary call has the same shape as the gamma of a vanilla call.
- For foreign exchange, paying one unit of domestic currency when the spot is above or below the strike is exactly a cash-or-nothing call or put, and paying one unit of foreign currency is exactly an asset-or-nothing call or put, giving digital values C = e^{-r_d T} N(d2) for the domestic payout and C = S e^{-r_f T} N(d1) for the foreign payout.
- The Black-Scholes assumptions are not all empirically valid, and blindly following the model exposes the user to unexpected risk; its most significant limitations are underestimating extreme moves (tail risk), assuming instant cost-less trading (liquidity risk), assuming a stationary process (volatility risk), assuming continuous time and trading (gap risk), and underpricing deep out-of-the-money while overpricing deep in-the-money options.
- Delta hedging alone suffices to hedge an option inside the Black-Scholes model, but in practice there are many other sources of risk.
- Black-Scholes pricing remains widely used because it is a useful approximation for the direction prices move when crossing critical points, a robust basis for more refined models, and reversible -- price can be treated as an input and volatility solved for, giving the implied volatility used as a quoting convention.
- If the Black-Scholes model held, a stock's implied volatility would be identical across all strikes and maturities; in practice the volatility surface is not flat, which is how the model can be tested and found wanting.
- The shape of the implied volatility curve depends on the underlying: equities are skewed, with implied volatility substantially higher for low strikes and slightly lower for high strikes than at-the-money; currencies are more symmetrical, lowest at-the-money and higher in both wings; commodities often behave the reverse of equities.
- The standard practice despite the volatility smile is to treat the volatility surface as a fact about the market and feed an implied volatility from it into a Black-Scholes valuation, an approach described as using "the wrong number in the wrong formula to get the right price".
- Black-Scholes cannot be applied directly to bonds because of pull-to-par: as the bond approaches maturity all its prices become known and its volatility falls, which the model does not reflect.
- Interest rate volatility can contribute significantly to an option's price, especially a long-dated one, because rates vary by tenor and over time while Black-Scholes takes a single constant rate.
- Black-Scholes assumes positive underlying prices and does not work directly when the underlying can go negative; practitioners then use a different model such as Bachelier's, or add a constant offset to the prices.
- The normality assumption of the Black-Scholes model does not capture extreme movements such as stock market crashes.
- The Black-Scholes delta, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying price, is N(d+) for a call and N(d+)-1 for a put -- equivalently -N(-d+) -- so a call's delta lies between 0 and 1 and a put's between -1 and 0.
- The Black-Scholes gamma, the second partial derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying price, is N'(d+)/(S sigma sqrt(T-t)), where N' is the standard normal density.
- The Black-Scholes vega, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to volatility, is S N'(d+) sqrt(T-t).
- The Black-Scholes theta, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to time, is -S N'(d+) sigma / (2 sqrt(T-t)) - r K e^{-r(T-t)} N(d-) for a call and -S N'(d+) sigma / (2 sqrt(T-t)) + r K e^{-r(T-t)} N(-d-) for a put: the two differ only in the sign of the second term.
- The Black-Scholes rho, the partial derivative of the option value with respect to the risk-free rate, is K(T-t) e^{-r(T-t)} N(d-) for a call and -K(T-t) e^{-r(T-t)} N(-d-) for a put.
- The Black-Scholes Greeks are available in closed form and are obtained by differentiating the Black-Scholes formula, which is why every sensitivity of the model is exactly computable rather than estimated numerically.
- The original Black-Scholes model assumes the stock pays no dividend, though trivial extensions of the model can accommodate a continuous dividend yield factor.
- Delta is the most important Greek because it usually carries the largest risk, and many traders zero their delta at the end of the day when they are not speculating on market direction, following the delta-neutral hedging approach Black-Scholes defines.
- Substituting N(d-) for N(d+) in the Black-Scholes formula yields a negative value for out-of-the-money call options, which is a direct demonstration that the naive reading of the two terms as one probability times one value is wrong.
- Barone-Adesi and Whaley approximate the American option by splitting the stochastic differential equation into the European option value plus the early exercise premium, then solving a quadratic for the premium under some assumptions; the solution requires finding the critical underlying price at which one is indifferent between exercising early and holding to maturity.
- Bjerksund and Stensland approximate the American option with a trigger-price exercise strategy: exercise is optimal once the underlying reaches the trigger price, and below it the option reduces to a European up-and-out call plus a rebate paid if it is knocked out before maturity; the method is computationally inexpensive and fast.
- The Black-Scholes model extends to variable but deterministic rates and volatilities and to European options on dividend-paying instruments, where closed-form solutions survive if the dividend is a known proportion of the stock price; American options and options on stocks paying a known cash dividend are the harder cases.
- Solving the Black-Scholes model for volatility across a set of durations and strike prices constructs the implied volatility surface, an application that amounts to a coordinate transformation from the price domain to the volatility domain.

[MUST CARRY — definition] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0001
  The Black-Scholes (or Black-Scholes-Merton) model is a mathematical model of the dynamics of a financial market containing derivative instruments, from whose parabolic partial differential equation one deduces the Black-Scholes formula: a theoretical price for European-style options that is unique given the security's risk, with the security's expected return replaced by the risk-neutral rate.

[MUST CARRY — definition] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0002
  Black-Scholes prices an option by hedging it: buying and selling the underlying asset continuously so as to eliminate risk, a technique called continuously revised delta hedging, which is the basis of the more complicated hedging strategies used by investment banks and hedge funds.

[MUST CARRY — definition, procedure, prohibition] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0003
  Volatility is the only Black-Scholes parameter that cannot be observed directly in the market; because the option value rises with it for both puts and calls, the formula can be inverted on observed option prices to produce a volatility surface, which is then used to calibrate other models.

[MUST CARRY — assumption] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0007
  Black-Scholes assumes the riskless asset earns a constant rate of return, the risk-free interest rate.

[MUST CARRY — assumption] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0008
  Black-Scholes assumes the stock price follows a geometric Brownian motion with constant drift and volatility; if drift and volatility vary with time a modified formula can still be derived, provided the volatility is not random.

[MUST CARRY — definition, formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0011
  The Black-Scholes equation is the parabolic partial differential equation governing the option price V(S,t), where S is the underlying price, t is time, sigma is volatility and r the risk-free rate: dV/dt + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + rS dV/dS - rV = 0.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0013
  The Black-Scholes call price for a non-dividend-paying stock is C(S_t,t) = N(d+)S_t - N(d-)K e^{-r(T-t)}, with d+ = [ln(S_t/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)(T-t)] / (sigma sqrt(T-t)) and d- = d+ - sigma sqrt(T-t).

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0014
  The Black-Scholes put price follows from put-call parity rather than a separate derivation: P(S_t,t) = K e^{-r(T-t)} - S_t + C(S_t,t) = N(-d-)K e^{-r(T-t)} - N(-d+)S_t.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0015
  The Black-Scholes formula is obtained by solving the Black-Scholes equation subject to the terminal and boundary conditions C(0,t)=0 for all t, C(S,t) ~ S - K e^{-r(T-t)} as S goes to infinity, and C(S,T)=max{S-K,0}, which is why the formula and the equation are consistent with each other.

[MUST CARRY — definition, formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0016
  In the Black-Scholes formula N(x) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, N(x) = (1/sqrt(2 pi)) times the integral of e^{-z^2/2} from minus infinity to x.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0017
  Time to maturity in the Black-Scholes notation is tau = T - t, the difference between the option's expiration time T and the current time t.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0018
  Introducing the discount factor D = e^{-r tau} and the forward price F = e^{r tau} S = S/D simplifies the Black-Scholes call to C(F,tau) = D[N(d+)F - N(d-)K], a special case of the Black '76 formula, in which d+ = [ln(F/K) + (1/2)sigma^2 tau] / (sigma sqrt(tau)).

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0019
  Put-call parity in forward terms is C - P = D(F - K) = S - DK, and it yields the put price P(F,tau) = D[N(-d-)K - N(-d+)F].

[MUST CARRY — prohibition] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0021
  Reading N(d+) and N(d-) as probabilities of the option expiring in the money is incorrect, because either both binaries expire in the money or neither does, so a single event cannot carry two different probabilities.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0023
  The (1/2)sigma^2 term that distinguishes d- from standardized moneyness m = ln(F/K)/(sigma sqrt(tau)) comes from the gap between the median and the mean of the log-normal distribution -- the same factor Ito's lemma produces for geometric Brownian motion.

[MUST CARRY — assumption, definition] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0024
  N(d-) is the probability that a Black-Scholes call is exercised when the asset is assumed to drift at the risk-free rate, whereas N(d+) has no simple probability interpretation; N(d+) is correctly read as the present value, at the risk-free rate, of the expected asset price at expiration conditional on that price exceeding the strike.

[MUST CARRY — definition, dependency] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0025
  The probabilities appearing in the Black-Scholes formula are measure-theoretic probabilities under the equivalent martingale (risk-neutral) measure, and neither is the true probability of expiring in the money under the real physical measure; computing that requires additional information, the drift.

[MUST CARRY — definition] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0026
  The Feynman-Kac formula says the appropriately discounted solution of the Black-Scholes PDE is a martingale, so the option price is the expected value of its discounted payoff -- the risk-neutrality approach, which prices options without any knowledge of PDEs.

[MUST CARRY — definition] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0029
  Gamma and vega take the same value for a call and a put on the same underlying, because the difference between a put and a call is a forward, which is linear in S and independent of sigma and therefore has zero gamma and zero vega.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0030
  Greeks are usually quoted scaled to the size of a likely parameter change: rho divided by 10,000 for a one-basis-point rate move, vega divided by 100 for a one-volatility-point move, and theta divided by 365 or 252 for one day of decay on calendar or trading days.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0031
  For an instrument paying a continuous dividend yield q, the Black-Scholes call is C(S_t,t) = e^{-r(T-t)}[F N(d1) - K N(d2)] with forward F = S_t e^{(r-q)(T-t)}, an assumption that is reasonable for options on indices.

[MUST CARRY — definition, formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0033
  Pricing an American option is the optimal stopping problem of choosing when to exercise, so the Black-Scholes equation becomes a variational inequality: the PDE expression is at most zero, the option value is at least the payoff H(S), and V(S,T) = H(S) at expiry.

[MUST CARRY — formula] u-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0034
  The American variational inequality generally has no closed-form solution, though an American call on a non-dividend-paying stock equals the European call, and the Roll-Geske-Whaley method solves the case of an American call with one dividend.

  assertions:
    - The Black-Scholes (or Black-Scholes-Merton) model is a mathematical model of the dynamics of a financial market containing derivative instruments, from whose parabolic partial differential equation one deduces the Black-Scholes formula: a theoretical price for European-style options that is unique given the security's risk, with the security's expected return replaced by the risk-neutral rate.   title: Black-Scholes: the equation, its boundary conditions and its closed-form solutions
  knowledge_state: authoritative
  operation: create_or_update
  summary: The core mathematics: the partial differential equation, the terminal and boundary conditions that pick out the call, the resulting call and put prices, the forward-price reformulation, and the notation the formulas use. Every formula is stated in full so it can be applied without returning to the source.
  assertions:
    - The Black-Scholes equation is the parabolic partial differential equation governing the option price V(S,t), where S is the underlying price, t is time, sigma is volatility and r the risk-free rate: dV/dt + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 d2V/dS2 + rS dV/dS - rV = 0.  [asmt-0011]
    - The Black-Scholes formula is obtained by solving the Black-Scholes equation subject to the terminal and boundary conditions C(0,t)=0 for all t, C(S,t) ~ S - K e^{-r(T-t)} as S goes to infinity, and C(S,T)=max{S-K,0}, which is why the formula and the equation are consistent with each other.  [asmt-0015]
    - The Black-Scholes call price for a non-dividend-paying stock is C(S_t,t) = N(d+)S_t - N(d-)K e^{-r(T-t)}, with d+ = [ln(S_t/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)(T-t)] / (sigma sqrt(T-t)) and d- = d+ - sigma sqrt(T-t).  [asmt-0013]
    - The Black-Scholes put price follows from put-call parity rather than a separate derivation: P(S_t,t) = K e^{-r(T-t)} - S_t + C(S_t,t) = N(-d-)K e^{-r(T-t)} - N(-d+)S_t.  [asmt-0014]
    - Introducing the discount factor D = e^{-r tau} and the forward price F = e^{r tau} S = S/D simplifies the Black-Scholes call to C(F,tau) = D[N(d+)F - N(d-)K], a special case of the Black '76 formula, in which d+ = [ln(F/K) + (1/2)sigma^2 tau] / (sigma sqrt(tau)).  [asmt-0018]
    - Put-call parity in forward terms is C - P = D(F - K) = S - DK, and it yields the put price P(F,tau) = D[N(-d-)K - N(-d+)F].  [asmt-0019]
    - In the Black-Scholes formula N(x) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, N(x) = (1/sqrt(2 pi)) times the integral of e^{-z^2/2} from minus infinity to x.  [asmt-0016]
    - Time to maturity in the Black-Scholes notation is tau = T - t, the difference between the option's expiration time T and the current time t.  [asmt-0017]
